cases.description: Ech0 before 4.4.3 fails to enforce scope-based authorization on nine comment panel admin endpoints, allowing access tokens with minimal scopes to perform full comment moderation operations. Attackers with a limited-scope access token can list, approve, reject, delete comments, and modify comment system settings by directly accessing the unprotected panel endpoints.
cases.mechanism: An admin-issued access JWT carrying only an unrelated minimal scope such as echo:read passed JWTAuthMiddleware and reached all nine /api/panel/comments routes because those AuthRouterGroup registrations lacked RequireScopes. The comment service then checked only the database user's admin/owner role, not the access token's scopes, allowing the limited token to read comments and settings, moderate or delete comments, change comment settings, and send test email.
cases.scope_statement: Attribution covers the audited AI-associated introducer bf994ebfd5fe2e16b85ff64ad25147abd9ba99d7 and advisory-linked remediation 6df5673010720847e35d8bb8f60403e2cc4ab313; unrelated repository changes are outside scope.

ai_provenance.note: Made-with: Cursor

code_evidence.summary: AI-generated panel endpoints omitted scope checks, letting minimal-scope tokens fully moderate comments and alter settings.

steps.title: AI change
steps.detail: feat(authz): enforce route-level scope checks for access tokens

steps.title: Fix
steps.detail: refactor(router): add middleware for authorization scopes on various routes

cases.research_status: ['CVE-2026-79672 / GHSA-x98j-gh4v-7p7g: Ech0 before 4.4.3 fails to enforce scope-based authorization on nine comment panel admin endpoints (CWE-862). Vendor advisory https://github.com/lin-snow/Ech0/security/advisories/GHSA-fwg7-53p4-g33c (same vulnerability; referenced by the CVE) names internal/router/comment.go panel routes, RequireScopes in internal/middleware/scope.go, and requireAdmin() role-only check.', "Panel routes first written in 975b98016352c8135fa8a787db6061a74991935c (parent 5819e01d0090f30194e076dc2360984f0fb33c6f has no comment.go). git log -S '/panel/comments' -- internal/router/comment.go starts there. No RequireScopes existed yet (git grep RequireScopes 975b9801 -- '*.go' empty). cases.description: Ech0 version 4.3.4 and earlier fails to reliably enforce scoped access token (least-privilege) restrictions on several privileged admin routes. Multiple privileged endpoints (e.g., /api/inbox, /api/panel/comments, /api/backup/export) omit scope checks and authorize based only on the user's admin role, and the backup export handler discards token scope metadata entirely. An attacker holding a deliberately limited (low-scope) admin access token can reach broader privileged functionality than intended, including reading the inbox and exporting a full database backup ZIP archive. Fixed in 4.4.3.
cases.mechanism: Ech0's scoped access tokens promised least privilege but privileged authorization was split among JWT authentication, opt-in RequireScopes route middleware, and service-level checks of the underlying account's IsAdmin bit. A deliberately narrow admin access token, such as echo:read, therefore authenticated to privileged routes that omitted RequireScopes, including /api/inbox and panel-comment routes. The public /api/backup/export path additionally reparsed a query JWT and rebuilt viewer state from only claims.Userid, discarding token type, scopes, audience, and JTI, so the backup service saw an unrestricted admin identity and returned the database/log ZIP.

comparison_hunks.annotation: The service-level token creation now runs validateAccessTokenRequest, which rejects empty names, unknown audiences, empty scope lists, and any scope that is not registered, and refuses admin-only scopes for non-admin users before minting the JWT.

CreateAccessToken stores the token type, JSON-encoded scopes, audience, and a fresh JTI on the token record, and writes those claims into the JWT itself, so the issued bearer token now carries the least-privilege metadata it previously lacked.

The access-token DTO gains Scopes and Audience fields. Because enforcement stayed opt-in on later routes, adding these fields minted narrow-scope tokens without actually restricting the privileged endpoints that skip the scope middleware.

The backup export handler previously reparsed a query token and rebuilt the viewer identity from only claims.Userid. That discarded token type, scopes, audience, and JTI, so a low-scope admin token reached the backup service as a full admin and exported the database ZIP.

cases.description: RequireScopes short-circuits with ctx.Next() whenever the JWT typ is session, before any scope or audience check. POST /login issues session tokens, so any authenticated non-admin satisfies JWTAuth/RequireAuth and then skips the only admin gate on routes that attach RequireScopes(admin:user|admin:settings) without a handler/service IsAdmin check. That lets a logged-in non-admin read GET /api/users (emails and admin flags), GET /api/system/logs, GET /api/system/visitor-stats, GET /api/system/check-update, and SSE /api/system/logs/stream. /ws/system/logs is registered on WSRouterGroup with no middleware; the handler only jwtUtil.ParseToken's the query token and never checks IsAdmin, scope, or audience, so the same session JWT tails live system logs.

cases.description: vLLM's video MediaIO merges unauthenticated request-level media_io_kwargs into the decode backend. VideoMediaIO.merge_kwargs() strips a requested video_backend/backend only when VIDEO_LOADER_REGISTRY.backend_requires_gpu(name) is true; that lookup defaults unknown names to False. DeepStream/NVDEC was implemented as DeepStreamVideoBackendMixin on the loader registered as "opencv" and was never registered with requires_gpu=True (unlike pynvvideocodec). A client can therefore set media_io_kwargs.video.backend=deepstream, pass the GPU-backend gate, and reach VideoBackend.load_bytes(). The DeepStream branch lazily constructs a process-wide DecodePool whose size is taken from request pool_size (clamped to 1–16; first request wins) and calls probe_metadata() for width/height but never _check_frame_pixel_limit(), so videos rejected by OpenCV/PyAV/TorchCodec/PyNvVideoCodec are GPU-decoded and starve concurrent work (partial CWE-400 DoS; CVSS 5.3).

+class DeepStreamVideoBackendMixin:
+    """NVIDIA DeepStream (NVDEC) GPU-decode codec utilities.
+
+    Decoding runs on a shared pool of daemon threads inside one CUDA
+    context (see the ``nvidia-deepstream-videodecode-cu13`` package). The
+    container bytes are pushed into an ``appsrc`` GStreamer pipeline, so no
+    local file path is required — HTTP and base64 sources decode identically
+    to local files.
+
+    Like the OpenCV/PyAV mixins, this provides only the codec layer.
+    Frame *selection* lives in the loader's
+    ``compute_frames_index_to_sample`` and arrives here as an explicit
+    list of frame indices.
+    """
+
+    # Process-wide lazy decode pool, shared across all DeepStream backends.
+    _pool: ClassVar[Any] = None
+    _pool_lock: ClassVar[Any] = None
+
+    @classmethod
+    def _get_pool(cls, pool_size: int | None = None):
+        """Lazy-initialize the shared decode pool on first use.
+
+        ``pool_size`` (number of decode worker threads) comes from
+        ``--media-io-kwargs`` (``{"video": {"pool_size": N}}``); when unset it
+        defaults to the existing ``VLLM_MEDIA_LOADING_THREAD_COUNT`` so no
+        DeepStream-specific env var is needed. The pool is a process-wide
+        singleton, so the first decode's value wins.
+        """
+        if cls._pool is not None:
+            return cls._pool
+        if cls._pool_lock is None:
+            cls._pool_lock = threading.Lock()
+        with cls._pool_lock:
+            if cls._pool is not None:
+                return cls._pool
+            import os
+
+            from nvidia.deepstream_videodecode import DecodePool
+
+            if pool_size is None:
+                pool_size = os.environ.get("VLLM_MEDIA_LOADING_THREAD_COUNT", 8)
+            pool_size = max(1, min(int(pool_size), 16))
+            logger.info(
+                "[DeepStream] initializing decode pool with %d workers",
+                pool_size,
+            )
+            cls._pool = DecodePool(num_workers=pool_size)
+            return cls._pool
+
+    @classmethod
+    def decode_indices(
+        cls,
+        data: bytes,
+        frame_indices: list[int],
+        source: VideoSourceMetadata,
+        codec: str = "",
+        pool_size: int | None = None,
+        timeout_sec: float = 120.0,
+    ) -> tuple[npt.NDArray, list[int]]:
+        """Decode the requested frame indices from raw container bytes.
+
+        The whole stream is decoded; the pool keeps exactly the frames whose
+        decode-order index is in ``frame_indices`` (1:1, frame-exact) and
+        sends EOS once the last one is matched.
+
+        ``codec`` (e.g. ``"h264"``/``"hevc"``) lets the pool keep its NVDEC
+        session warm across same-codec streams and rebuild only on a codec
+        change. Frames are returned as a CPU NHWC uint8 array so the
+        upstream multimodal parser sees the same shape as the other
+        backends.
+        """
+        if not frame_indices:
+            raise ValueError("DeepStream backend received no frame indices")
+
+        result = cls._get_pool(pool_size).decode(
+            data,
+            target_indices=frame_indices,
+            codec=codec,
+            max_frames=len(frame_indices),
+            timeout_sec=timeout_sec,
+        )
+        if result.error:
+            raise ValueError(f"DeepStream decode failed: {result.error}")
+        if result.frames is None or result.n_kept == 0:

cases.description: Repo.blame() and Repo.blame_incremental() collect a caller-controlled rev as an option candidate and then pass that value to git blame before the '--' path separator. The guard introduced for unsafe revision options listed only the write options --output/-o, so --contents=<path> and -S=<path> passed with allow_unsafe_options=False. Git blame treats those as file-input options, and its porcelain result exposes victim-file lines to the API caller.
cases.mechanism: The guard checked a short denylist before passing the caller-controlled revision to git blame. File-input options remained accepted before the path separator, so Git read the chosen victim file and returned its contents through blame output.

code_evidence.summary: AI-written GitPython blame validation blocked only output options but missed file-reading options, allowing callers to read arbitrary files through a revision argument.

steps.title: AI change
steps.detail: fix: Guard unsafe git command options (GHSA-956x-8gvw-wg5v)

steps.title: Security fix
steps.detail: The fix extends blame validation to reject the file-reading --contents, -S, and --ignore-revs-file options before the caller-controlled revision reaches git blame, while retaining the explicit unsafe-options opt-out.

cases.description: Ech0 before 4.4.3 protects the PUT /user endpoint with the profile:read scope, a read-only scope, but allows write operations including password changes. An attacker with an admin's profile:read access token can change the admin's password and login to obtain an unrestricted session token that bypasses all scope enforcement.
cases.mechanism: A scoped access token carrying only profile:read is accepted by PUT /user because that mutating route is guarded by RequireScopes(ScopeProfileRead). UpdateUser uses the token viewer's administrator identity and permits a supplied password to replace that administrator's password. The attacker can then log in with the replacement password; login issues a session JWT, and RequireScopes deliberately bypasses scope checks for session tokens, yielding unrestricted administrator access.

comparison_hunks.annotation: The middleware test asserts that a token holding only profile:read is refused on routes that demand profile:write, pinning down the separation between read and write scopes at the handler boundary.

Every mutating profile route now swaps RequireScopes(ScopeProfileRead) for RequireScopes(ScopeProfileWrite). A read-scoped token can no longer change the password, and session JWTs remain the only way to reach these endpoints.

cases.description: Paperclip before 0.3.1 in default local_trusted mode fails to validate Host headers, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary commands via DNS rebinding. An attacker can craft a malicious webpage that, when visited by a developer running Paperclip locally, uses DNS rebinding to make authenticated API requests and execute commands through the process adapter.
cases.mechanism: A page served from an attacker-controlled DNS name can retain its browser origin while DNS rebinding moves the connection to a victim's loopback Paperclip server. Paperclip's missing Host-header gate in default private local_trusted mode allowed that request to receive the implicit instance-admin board actor, create/configure a process-adapter agent with attacker-controlled command and arguments, and invoke its heartbeat/wakeup path, which passed the stored configuration to child_process.spawn as the Paperclip OS user.

steps.detail: Enables the private-hostname guard for local_trusted deployments as well as authenticated private deployments, so requests with unapproved Host headers are rejected before actor assignment.

comparison_hunks.annotation: Adds implicit board-actor middleware that sets req.actor to a fixed board identity and only promotes a caller to a real API-key actor when the bearer token hashes to a live non-revoked key, otherwise falling through as board.
Adds a heartbeat service able to spawn and manage child processes for monitored agents, a critical building block of the RCE/authorization chain.
Mounts company and expanded agent routes behind the implicit board-actor middleware, extending authenticated surface without Host validation.
The fix centralizes when the private-hostname guard should be enabled, including local_trusted deployments, so the same host-based protection applies broadly.

cases.research_status: The first-party advisory https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/security/advisories/GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7 identifies the three necessary flaws and explicitly says that enabling Host validation for local_trusted kills the attack; it reports affected <0.3.1 and patched None. Direct-parent checks `git cat-file -e 8c830eae70a14723749828f0ce5d9ae435270e9c:server/src/services/heartbeat.ts` and the analogous auth.ts check both exit 128 because the paths are absent, while `git diff-tree --name-status -r abadd469...` reports both paths added. `git cat-file commit abadd469...` shows one parent and the exact Claude Opus 4.6 co-author trailer. The assigned fix disagreement is between the primary's direct_fix_sha edeec965f84e4376c42e93761823ff1b959a8302 and the reviewer's direct_fix_sha 32a9165ddf6308f3b46eae0653b6f583e502e538 (both agree on landed fix_sha 32a9165...). `git show edeec965... -- server/src/app.ts server/src/__tests__/app-private-hostname-gate.test.ts` shows the original direct change: it adds shouldEnablePrivateHostnameGuard, makes local_trusted enable the existing guard, and adds a local_trusted regression case; its parent c92db0a173a10aa88040f16a155447e95b820f76 still has only `authenticated && private`. The source ancestry is edeec965... -> eb3c367... -> 036421f... -> 4f91d94..., where 4f91d94d35563f9c5c02bf45e5a5ee1271290310 refines the predicate to private exposure. `git diff 4f91d94... 32a9165... -- server/src/app.ts server/src/__tests__/app-private-hostname-gate.test.ts` is empty, proving that 32a9165... lands the final source-branch fix, but `git show --stat 32a9165...` shows a 39-file GitHub squash containing unrelated issue/editor and wakeup work; it is therefore the landed fix, not the direct source commit. Both c92db0a... and the squash parent 50cd76d8a3f2fc06d1a5af63840abd3d7a1bcd02 retain the vulnerable authenticated-private-only gate. Version checks resolve the boundary: v0.3.1 peels to 63c62e3ada077bac45292f3d2779bd48a8831cda and contains the BIC but not the fix; `git for-each-ref --contains=32a9165... --sort=version:refname` identifies v2026.416.0, peeled commit b8725c52eff66cdea8cb223f1ca885475a254468, as the first stable v* tag containing the landed fix. The manipulation of the argument exec results in code injection. The attack may be performed from remote. The exploit has been made public and could be used. cases.mechanism: When the optional webhook server is enabled, it listens on all interfaces and treats an empty configured token as authenticated. An unauthenticated remote POST to the configured hook path can therefore supply a JSON exec value; handleHook dispatches that value to executeShell, which passes it as the command string to the configured shell. Thus an enabled deployment with the documented empty-token setting exposes arbitrary command execution in the cc-connect process context.

unpatched.reason: The advisory remained unpatched at the audited repository head, so no remediation commit is attributed; the reported GitHub issue was closed automatically due to inactivity, meaning no upstream fix was ever merged.

potential_fix.approach: Fail closed in the webhook authenticator: treat an empty or whitespace-only configured token as invalid at startup and in Authenticate, returning 401 for every request to the hook path when no non-empty token is configured; additionally require a constant-time comparison of the presented token against the configured non-empty token in handleHook before dispatching the JSON exec value to executeShell.
potential_fix.rationale: The RCE sink is only reachable because an empty configured token is treated as authenticated, letting an unauthenticated remote POST reach handleHook and flow a supplied exec value into executeShell. Rejecting every request when the token is empty (and requiring a valid token match) removes the authenticated-but-keyless state, so the exec payload can never reach the shell without a secret.

cases.description: A vulnerability was identified in chenhg5 cc-connect up to 1.4.1. This affects the function shellExecCommand of the file core/engine.go of the component Management API. Such manipulation of the argument exec leads to os command injection. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The exploit is publicly available and might be used. The reported GitHub issue was closed automatically due to inactivity.
cases.mechanism: When the Management API is enabled with its token omitted or empty, its middleware treats every request as authenticated and its HTTP server listens on all interfaces. A remote caller can POST an arbitrary exec string to /api/v1/cron; that string is persisted as CronJob.Exec and executed by the cron scheduler through shellExecCommand with the shell command flag (-c on Unix). Scheduled execution is sufficient for RCE, and later commit c580b68716a7cdc6a0e6702e5782c17d074a7978 also added POST /api/v1/cron/{id}/exec for immediate execution. No shell metacharacter neutralization or command allowlist intervenes.

BIC-only AI evidence comes from git cat-file commit c2681402 and the public commit object at https://github.com/chenhg5/cc-connect/commit/c2681402a7686294174a263e31245a52d4fea380, which carry the llmgit and Claude co-author markers.

unpatched.reason: The advisory remained unpatched at the audited repository head, so no remediation commit is attributed; the reported GitHub issue was closed automatically due to inactivity.

potential_fix.approach: (1) Make the Management API middleware fail closed: reject all requests with HTTP 401 when the configured token is omitted or empty instead of treating every request as authenticated. (2) At the execution boundary, validate CronJob.Exec before shellExecCommand invokes `sh -c`: reject any value containing shell metacharacters and/or match it against an allowlist of safe command names, on both the persisted /api/v1/cron path and the immediate /api/v1/cron/{id}/exec path.
potential_fix.rationale: Remote RCE requires both an unauthenticated route (a) and the raw Exec string being handed to the shell (b). Failing closed on an empty token removes the unauthenticated write to CronJob.Exec, and validating/allowlisting the Exec string at the scheduler boundary neutralizes the CWE-77 injection sink even if a caller is authenticated.

steps.title: AI change
steps.detail: feat(workflow-sdk): integrate Zod schema validation into validate()

steps.title: Security fix
steps.detail: Rejects separators, NULs, and dot path components in node types, then resolves each schema module's real path and loads it only when it remains inside the configured nodes directory.

comparison_hunks.annotation: The workflow schema validator dynamically loads Zod schema files from ~/.n8n/generated-types/, building the require path from the node type name. When that name is not sanitized, a crafted node type can escape the schemas directory and load an attacker-chosen module.

validateNodeConfig wires the schema check into workflow validation and adds an INVALID_PARAMETER result type, exposing the new dynamically-loaded schema path to every node configuration that flows through the SDK.

The validator test imports loadSchema, setSchemaBasePath, and getSchemaBasePath, confirming that the schema base directory is configurable at runtime and that loading is keyed by caller-supplied node identifiers.

The fix validates each node-type-derived path component with isSafePathComponent and resolves the final path with realpathSync, then verifies the resolved file stays inside the schemas base directory before requiring it.

cases.description: The JavaScript Code node executes user code in the task-runner Node VM with host objects injected into the sandbox. `$input.constructor.constructor.prototype` is the host Function.prototype. The freeze loop only froze prototypes with `typeof === 'object'`, but `typeof Function.prototype === 'function'`, so that prototype stayed mutable. An authenticated user who can create and execute workflows can pollute Function.prototype, recover host globalThis, and complete a sandbox escape when allowlisted imports (NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN / NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL) supply gadgets. CWE-1321. Patched in 1.123.69, 2.33.4, and 2.34.1 by freezing function-typed prototypes as well (`isFreezable` = object or function).

cases.description: When phpMyFAQ uses PostgreSQL through the native pgsql PHP extension, public FAQ search interpolates the unauthenticated `search` parameter into `Pgsql::search()` as `(%s) ILIKE ('%%%s%%')` after `SearchDatabase::escapeLikeWildcards()`. That helper prefixes user `%` and `_` with `|`, which only disables LIKE wildcards if the SQL also declares `ESCAPE '|'`. Native `Pgsql.php` did not: after the BIC it had no matching ESCAPE clause (PostgreSQL default escape is backslash), and after the later 4.1 merge it declared `ESCAPE '='`. In both states `|` is a literal, so attacker-supplied `%`/`_` stay active wildcards, forcing maximally broad ILIKE matches and expensive sequential scans (availability DoS). Quotes are still passed through `getDb()->escape()`, so this is not quote-breaking SQL injection. The PDO sibling `PdoPgsql.php` declares `ESCAPE '|'` and is not affected.

code_evidence.summary: Copilot SWE-agent changed wildcard escaping without matching native PostgreSQL SQL, so unauthenticated searches could force broad scans and degrade availability.

steps.title: AI change
steps.detail: fix: use pipe character as LIKE ESCAPE to work across all databases

steps.title: Fix
steps.detail: fix(search): align native pgsql LIKE ESCAPE character with the wildcard escaper

candidate_hunks.annotation: The flawed mechanism was first written by Copilot SWE-agent commit 086c8ad58f91a8e34ea27fabd1ba9ca0b2487f42 (GitHub PR 4180 rebase onto main), which changed `escapeLikeWildcards()` and the PDO/generic LIKE clauses from backslash to `|` “to work across all databases” but left native `Pgsql.php` untouched. That file already called the shared escaper while emitting `ILIKE ('%%%s%%')` with no ESCAPE clause. At the immediate parent the escaper still used `\`, matching PostgreSQL’s default LIKE escape, so native wildcard neutralization still held. After 086c the native backend’s escaping is a no-op. Merge 8853a0fa8 later brought 4.1’s consistent `ESCAPE '='` rewrite (df54d00ce) onto main’s `|` escaper, which is the exact `'='` vs `'|'` pair in GHSA-5hx6-c293-588h / CVE-2026-76212; that merge is an aggregate overlay, not the first write. 4.1.5–4.1.7 keep matching `'='`/`'='` and do not contain this mismatch.

cases.description: openssl_encrypt versions before 1.4.0 contain an information disclosure vulnerability in the /ready endpoint that returns full database exception strings to unauthenticated callers. Attackers can trigger database errors to extract sensitive information including hostnames, IP addresses, connection parameters, and potentially credentials from exception messages.
cases.mechanism: The FastAPI GET /ready route performs an SQLAlchemy connection/query check without authentication and catches every resulting exception, then places str(e) directly in the JSON response's reason field. A remote unauthenticated caller that causes or observes a database failure can therefore receive driver and connection details, including database hostnames, IP addresses, ports, parameters, versions, and potentially credentials embedded in an error.
cases.scope_statement: Attribution covers the audited AI-associated introducer 8170b3e0be064cdaddbc8ef51c17e21c42d2d3f4 and advisory-linked remediation 7aa8787f4de2e9a23f58fca067bb16c4c69d28bb; unrelated repository changes are outside scope.

+

+

+
+# Configure logging

+)
+
+logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
+
+
+@asynccontextmanager
+async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
+    """
+    Lifespan event handler for FastAPI.

cases.description: openssl_encrypt versions before 1.4.0 contain hardcoded default JWT signing secrets in config.py that pass validation checks. Attackers with access to source code can forge valid JWT tokens for any client_id to gain authenticated access to keyserver and telemetry APIs.
cases.mechanism: The unified FastAPI server supplied two publicly known, >=32-character defaults for KEYSERVER_TOKEN_SECRET and TELEMETRY_TOKEN_SECRET. validate_config() checked only length and cross-module inequality, so an operator who did not override the environment variables started the production server with those known HS256 signing keys. TokenAuth.verify_token() accepted a JWT when its signature and module issuer matched and returned the attacker-chosen sub/client_id without requiring that client to exist, allowing source-aware attackers to mint bearer tokens that passed the keyserver or telemetry route dependencies.

cases.description: openssl_encrypt versions before 1.4.0 contain a sandbox bypass vulnerability where the plugin sandbox fails to restrict alternative file access methods like pathlib.Path and io.open. Attackers can import pathlib or io modules to read and write arbitrary files, completely bypassing the restricted_open file access controls.
cases.mechanism: A plugin executing without PluginCapability.READ_FILES was supposed to be confined to the sandbox temporary directory and explicitly safe paths. The sandbox enforced that policy only by replacing builtins.open with restricted_open. Plugin code could instead import pathlib or io and call pathlib.Path.read_text/read_bytes/write_text/write_bytes/open or io.open; those independent entry points never reached restricted_open, so the plugin could read or modify arbitrary host files, for example Path('/etc/passwd').read_text(), despite lacking the file capability. The repository advisory specifically describes the bypass in threading mode and notes that process isolation had a separate broader restriction failure.

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""
+Plugin Sandbox for OpenSSL Encrypt
+
+This module provides security sandboxing for plugin execution, ensuring
+plugins cannot access sensitive data, perform unauthorized operations,
+or consume excessive resources.
+
+Security Features:
+- Resource limits (memory, execution time)
+- Capability enforcement
+- File system access restrictions
+- Network access controls
+- Process isolation where possible
+"""
+
+import gc
+import logging
+import multiprocessing
+import os
+import resource
+import signal
+import sys
+import tempfile
+import threading
+import time
+from contextlib import contextmanager
+from typing import Any, Dict, Optional
+
+from .plugin_base import BasePlugin, PluginCapability, PluginResult, PluginSecurityContext
+
+logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
+
+
+class ResourceMonitor:
+    """Monitor plugin resource usage during execution."""
+
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.start_memory = 0
+        self.peak_memory = 0
+        self.start_time = 0
+        self.execution_time = 0
+        self.monitoring = False
+
+    def start(self):
+        """Start resource monitoring."""
+        self.start_memory = self._get_memory_usage()
+        self.peak_memory = self.start_memory
+        self.start_time = time.time()
+        self.monitoring = True
+
+    def stop(self):
+        """Stop resource monitoring."""
+        if self.monitoring:
+            self.execution_time = time.time() - self.start_time
+            self.monitoring = False
+
+    def update_peak_memory(self):
+        """Update peak memory usage."""
+        if self.monitoring:
+            current_memory = self._get_memory_usage()
+            if current_memory > self.peak_memory:
+                self.peak_memory = current_memory
+
+    def get_stats(self) -> Dict[str, float]:
+        """Get resource usage statistics."""
+        return {
+            "memory_start_mb": self.start_memory / (1024 * 1024),
+            "memory_peak_mb": self.peak_memory / (1024 * 1024),
+            "memory_used_mb": (self.peak_memory - self.start_memory) / (1024 * 1024),
+            "execution_time_s": self.execution_time,
+        }
+
+    @staticmethod
+    def _get_memory_usage() -> int:
+        """Get current memory usage in bytes."""
+        try:
+            # Try to get RSS (Resident Set Size) on Unix systems
+            if hasattr(resource, "RUSAGE_SELF"):
+                usage = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF)
+                # On Linux, ru_maxrss is in KB, on BSD systems it's in bytes
+                if sys.platform == "linux":
+                    return usage.ru_maxrss * 1024
+                else:
+                    return usage.ru_maxrss
+            else:
+                # Fallback for systems without resource module
+                import psutil
+

cases.research_status: First-party advisory https://github.com/jahlives/openssl_encrypt/security/advisories/GHSA-mcjj-qw7m-j3cp identifies openssl_encrypt/modules/plugin_system/plugin_sandbox.py, demonstrates Path('/etc/passwd').read_text(), states the affected range as <1.4.0, and names d0be3e9 as the fix. In the validated clone, `git log d0be3e9^ -L 479,512:openssl_encrypt/modules/plugin_system/plugin_sandbox.py` follows the vulnerable function through formatting and policy changes to 8a5ed7e62417441ed98b39481ac1a47510c1a9ef, whose added lines 217-251 call _restrict_file_operations when READ_FILES is absent and replace only builtins.open. Independent `git log --all -S'builtins.open = restricted_open' -- openssl_encrypt/modules/plugin_system/plugin_sandbox.py` and `-S'def _restrict_file_operations'` each return only 8a5ed7e62417441ed98b39481ac1a47510c1a9ef. `git diff --name-status 649f737a9f04645508d079c0c772a8a2b4c7457a 8a5ed7e62417441ed98b39481ac1a47510c1a9ef -- openssl_encrypt/modules/plugin_system/plugin_sandbox.py` reports `A`, directly proving the entire vulnerable file and mechanism are absent from the immediate parent tree. `git cat-file -p 8a5ed7e62417441ed98b39481ac1a47510c1a9ef` proves the one-parent topology, human author/committer, Claude Code generation line, and Claude co-author trailer. `git show d0be3e989b1632eadb68e17d07294cbf9ac57c1f` shows the direct repair: save and replace io.open plus pathlib.Path.open/read_text/read_bytes/write_text/write_bytes/unlink/mkdir/rmdir, route each through the sandbox path check, and restore every original method afterward. Its immediate parent e0c999ea44429e8de00b4acb3ba570efdc733092 had added pathlib and io to shared blocked-module constants as precursor hardening, while d0be3e989b1632eadb68e17d07294cbf9ac57c1f is the advisory-named commit that directly interposes the bypassing APIs. `git tag --contains` places the BIC first in v1.3.0 (and all v1.3.x tags) but not v1.2.1, and places the fix first in v1.4.0 and later tags, matching the patched boundary.

cases.description: openssl_encrypt versions before 1.4.0 contain an arbitrary code execution vulnerability in the Whirlpool hash implementation that uses broad glob patterns to load .so modules without integrity verification. Attackers can place malicious .so files matching the whirlpool*py313*.so pattern in site-packages directories to achieve native code execution when the module is loaded.

+"""
+Module to handle the compatibility of Whirlpool hash library across Python versions.
+"""
+
+import os
+import sys
+import importlib.util
+import sysconfig
+import site
+import glob
+import logging
+from pathlib import Path
+import subprocess
+import platform
+
+# Set up logging
+logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
+logger = logging.getLogger("setup_whirlpool")
+
+
+def find_whirlpool_modules():
+    """Find all Whirlpool modules installed in the system."""
+    whirlpool_modules = []
+    
+    # Get all site-packages directories
+    site_packages = set()
+    site_packages.add(sysconfig.get_path('purelib'))
+    site_packages.add(sysconfig.get_path('platlib'))
+    
+    # Add user site-packages
+    user_site = site.getusersitepackages()
+    if isinstance(user_site, str):
+        site_packages.add(user_site)
+    elif isinstance(user_site, list):
+        site_packages.update(user_site)
+    
+    # Check for modules in all site-packages
+    for site_pkg in site_packages:
+        if not os.path.exists(site_pkg):
+            continue
+        
+        # Look for any whirlpool-related files
+        whirlpool_files = []
+        pattern = os.path.join(site_pkg, "whirlpool*.so")
+        whirlpool_files.extend(glob.glob(pattern))
+        
+        pattern = os.path.join(site_pkg, "pywhirlpool*.so")
+        whirlpool_files.extend(glob.glob(pattern))
+        
+        # For Python 3.11+, look for the py311 variant
+        pattern = os.path.join(site_pkg, "whirlpool-py311*.so")
+        whirlpool_files.extend(glob.glob(pattern))
+        
+        # For Windows
+        pattern = os.path.join(site_pkg, "whirlpool*.pyd")
+        whirlpool_files.extend(glob.glob(pattern))
+        
+        pattern = os.path.join(site_pkg, "pywhirlpool*.pyd")
+        whirlpool_files.extend(glob.glob(pattern))
+        
+        # Add all found modules to the list
+        whirlpool_modules.extend(whirlpool_files)
+    
+    return whirlpool_modules
+
+
+def create_whirlpool_symlink():
+    """Create a symbolic link to the appropriate Whirlpool module."""
+    whirlpool_modules = find_whirlpool_modules()

+    
+    # Check if we already have a working module

A different authenticated client holding a target-valid signature can therefore revoke the owner's key.
cases.mechanism: The unified keyserver stored the uploader as owner_client_id and passed the authenticated client_id into revoke_key, but the AI-coauthored first write never compared them before setting revoked. openssl_encrypt 1.4.2 removes the complete server surface; the history-filtered successor later adds the missing owner check and focused denial tests.

cases.description: TOTPService.verify_code consults a class-level TOTPRateLimiter whose attempt and lockout maps are process-local dictionaries (later wrapped as unused-by-default InMemoryBackend). Multiple workers enforce independent counters and a restart discards them, so distributed or post-restart TOTP guesses bypass the nominal 5-attempt/15-minute lockout.
cases.mechanism: The remediation added a per-process guard instead of shared persistent state. Each worker counted independently and restarts erased counters; a later database backend existed but production code never selected it.

cases.description: PluginImportGuard is a sys.meta_path hook plus a sys.modules hider that is supposed to block dangerous imports at plugin runtime. Its denylist is CWE-184-incomplete: ALWAYS_BLOCKED is only {ctypes, __builtin__, __builtins__} and CAPABILITY_GATED adds subprocess (always), os (always), and socket (NETWORK_ACCESS). _should_block_module() returns False for every other top-level name, so find_module()/find_spec() do not raise and hide_dangerous_modules() never removes those names from sys.modules. After 50bec5d the AST analyzer's DANGEROUS_MODULES independently treats sys, shutil, multiprocessing, importlib, pickle, shelve, pty, fcntl, pwd, grp, signal, resource, pipes, popen2, and platform as never-importable; an attacker who bypasses that static pass (string obfuscation, encoding, or __import__ indirection) can therefore import those modules at runtime and reach arbitrary code execution (pickle.__reduce__, importlib, sys.modules, shutil, multiprocessing). Direct `import pickle`/`import sys` is the sink; AST is only the bypassable outer check.
cases.mechanism: PluginImportGuard is a sys.meta_path hook plus a sys.modules hider that is supposed to block dangerous imports at plugin runtime. Its denylist is CWE-184-incomplete: ALWAYS_BLOCKED is only {ctypes, __builtin__, __builtins__} and CAPABILITY_GATED adds subprocess (always), os (always), and socket (NETWORK_ACCESS). _should_block_module() returns False for every other top-level name, so find_module()/find_spec() do not raise and hide_dangerous_modules() never removes those names from sys.modules. After 50bec5d the AST analyzer's DANGEROUS_MODULES independently treats sys, shutil, multiprocessing, importlib, pickle, shelve, pty, fcntl, pwd, grp, signal, resource, pipes, popen2, and platform as never-importable; an attacker who bypasses that static pass (string obfuscation, encoding, or __import__ indirection) can therefore import those modules at runtime and reach arbitrary code execution (pickle.__reduce__, importlib, sys.modules, shutil, multiprocessing). Direct `import pickle`/`import sys` is the sink; AST is only the bypassable outer check.
cases.scope_statement: The finding covers the plugin import-policy mismatch first created by 8a5ed7e6, not the separate file-access advisory that shares the feature commit.

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""
+Plugin Sandbox for OpenSSL Encrypt
+
+This module provides security sandboxing for plugin execution, ensuring
+plugins cannot access sensitive data, perform unauthorized operations,
+or consume excessive resources.
+
+Security Features:
+- Resource limits (memory, execution time)
+- Capability enforcement
+- File system access restrictions
+- Network access controls
+- Process isolation where possible
+"""
+
+import gc
+import logging
+import multiprocessing
+import os
+import resource
+import signal
+import sys
+import tempfile
+import threading
+import time
+from contextlib import contextmanager
+from typing import Any, Dict, Optional
+
+from .plugin_base import BasePlugin, PluginCapability, PluginResult, PluginSecurityContext
+
+logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
+
+
+class ResourceMonitor:
+    """Monitor plugin resource usage during execution."""
+
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.start_memory = 0
+        self.peak_memory = 0
+        self.start_time = 0
+        self.execution_time = 0
+        self.monitoring = False
+
+    def start(self):
+        """Start resource monitoring."""
+        self.start_memory = self._get_memory_usage()
+        self.peak_memory = self.start_memory
+        self.start_time = time.time()
+        self.monitoring = True
+
+    def stop(self):
+        """Stop resource monitoring."""
+        if self.monitoring:
+            self.execution_time = time.time() - self.start_time
+            self.monitoring = False
+
+    def update_peak_memory(self):
+        """Update peak memory usage."""
+        if self.monitoring:
+            current_memory = self._get_memory_usage()
+            if current_memory > self.peak_memory:
+                self.peak_memory = current_memory
+
+    def get_stats(self) -> Dict[str, float]:
+        """Get resource usage statistics."""
+        return {
+            "memory_start_mb": self.start_memory / (1024 * 1024),
+            "memory_peak_mb": self.peak_memory / (1024 * 1024),
+            "memory_used_mb": (self.peak_memory - self.start_memory) / (1024 * 1024),
+            "execution_time_s": self.execution_time,
+        }
+
+    @staticmethod
+    def _get_memory_usage() -> int:
+        """Get current memory usage in bytes."""
+        try:
+            # Try to get RSS (Resident Set Size) on Unix systems
+            if hasattr(resource, "RUSAGE_SELF"):
+                usage = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF)
+                # On Linux, ru_maxrss is in KB, on BSD systems it's in bytes
+                if sys.platform == "linux":
+                    return usage.ru_maxrss * 1024
+                else:
+                    return usage.ru_maxrss
+            else:
+                # Fallback for systems without resource module
+                import psutil
+

cases.description: openssl_encrypt versions before 1.4.0 contain a logging bug in restore_hidden_modules() that logs module counts after clearing, always showing zero restored modules and corrupting audit trails. Additionally, a race condition exists between module hiding and import hook installation where another thread could re-import blocked modules in multi-threaded environments.
cases.mechanism: PluginImportGuard.restore_hidden_modules() restored entries, cleared self.hidden_modules, and only then logged len(self.hidden_modules), so every restoration audit event falsely reported zero. The same guard removed blocked modules from sys.modules before inserting itself into sys.meta_path; a concurrent thread could re-import a removed module in that interval, repopulating sys.modules and making the supposedly blocked module reachable during plugin execution.
cases.scope_statement: Attribution covers the audited AI-associated introducer e588aaa3a53ef291406b02745c20fdea8cea7f7c and advisory-linked remediation 85cdb6bedf3a0fbfb49e2f2e29cd66f1f36f3101; unrelated repository changes are outside scope.

+class PluginImportGuard:
+    """
+    Import hook to block dangerous module imports in plugin code.
+
+    Prevents plugins from importing restricted modules that could be used
+    to bypass sandbox restrictions (e.g., subprocess, os, socket).
+
+    Installed in sys.meta_path before plugin execution.
+    Also temporarily removes dangerous modules from sys.modules to prevent
+    access to already-imported modules.
+    """
+
+    # Modules that should always be blocked
+    ALWAYS_BLOCKED = {
+        'ctypes',         # Load arbitrary C code
+        '__builtin__',    # Access to builtins
+        '__builtins__',   # Access to builtins
+    }
+
+    # Modules that are blocked unless specific capability is granted
+    CAPABILITY_GATED = {
+        'subprocess': None,  # Always blocked (no capability for this)
+        'os': None,          # Always blocked (contains os.system, etc.)
+        'socket': PluginCapability.NETWORK_ACCESS,  # Allowed with NETWORK_ACCESS
+    }
+
+    def __init__(self, context: PluginSecurityContext = None):
+        """Initialize the import guard.
+
+        Args:
+            context: Plugin security context with capabilities
+        """
+        self.context = context
+        self.hidden_modules = {}
+
+    def _should_block_module(self, module_name: str) -> bool:
+        """Check if a module should be blocked based on capabilities.
+
+        Args:
+            module_name: Name of the module to check
+
+        Returns:
+            True if module should be blocked, False if allowed
+        """
+        # Always block certain modules
+        if module_name in self.ALWAYS_BLOCKED:
+            return True
+
+        # Check capability-gated modules
+        if module_name in self.CAPABILITY_GATED:
+            required_capability = self.CAPABILITY_GATED[module_name]
+            # If no capability can grant access (None), always block
+            if required_capability is None:
+                return True
+            # If capability is granted, allow access
+            if self.context and required_capability in self.context.capabilities:
+                return False
+            # Otherwise, block
+            return True
+
+        return False
+
+    def hide_dangerous_modules(self):
+        """
+        Remove dangerous modules from sys.modules to prevent access.
+
+        Saves removed modules so they can be restored later.
+        """
+        # Get all modules that should be blocked
+        modules_to_hide = set(self.ALWAYS_BLOCKED) | set(self.CAPABILITY_GATED.keys())
+
+        for module_name in modules_to_hide:
+            # Check if module should actually be blocked based on capabilities
+            if self._should_block_module(module_name) and module_name in sys.modules:
+                self.hidden_modules[module_name] = sys.modules[module_name]
+                del sys.modules[module_name]
+                logger.debug(f"Hidden module from sys.modules: {module_name}")
+
+    def restore_hidden_modules(self):
+        """Restore previously hidden modules to sys.modules."""
+        for module_name, module in self.hidden_modules.items():
+            sys.modules[module_name] = module
+        self.hidden_modules.clear()
+        logger.debug(f"Restored {len(self.hidden_modules)} hidden modules")
+
+    def find_module(self, fullname, path=None):

cases.research_status: The logging subissue is patched by the advisory-named 85cdb6bedf3a0fbfb49e2f2e29cd66f1f36f3101, but the repository does not show a complete patch for the advisory's broader arbitrary-thread re-import window: 85c leaves deletion before hook installation and importing threads do not acquire `_modules_lock`. Also, tag ancestry disproves the published '<1.4.0' release range as written because pre-1.4.0 tags lack the guard and v1.4.0 already includes 85c. These are lifecycle/advisory defects, not gaps in BIC or AI attribution evidence. The first-party advisory https://github.com/jahlives/openssl_encrypt/security/advisories/GHSA-43r4-3hf9-m84q identifies openssl_encrypt/modules/plugin_system/plugin_sandbox.py, the clear-before-log defect, the hide/import-hook race, affected range <1.4.0, and direct fix 85cdb6b. `git log -L '/^    def restore_hidden_modules/,/^    def find_module/':openssl_encrypt/modules/plugin_system/plugin_sandbox.py 85cdb6b...` has exactly the relevant origin e588aaa3a53ef291406b02745c20fdea8cea7f7c and change 85cdb6bedf3a0fbfb49e2f2e29cd66f1f36f3101; `git log --all -S'Restored {len(self.hidden_modules)}' -- .../plugin_sandbox.py` likewise shows e588 adding and 85c removing the vulnerable expression. The e588 patch adds the entire PluginImportGuard, stores/deletes blocked sys.modules entries, clears hidden_modules before logging its length, then calls import_guard.hide_dangerous_modules() before sys.meta_path.insert(). Direct parent-tree command `git grep -n -e 'class PluginImportGuard' -e 'restore_hidden_modules' -e 'hide_dangerous_modules' 5f8412ee11ac37e57190d6af4fe02f2cf7f2a5bd -- openssl_encrypt/modules/plugin_system/plugin_sandbox.py` returned no matches (exit 1), while the e588 diff is a 131-line addition containing the mechanism. `git cat-file commit e588...` proves the single parent, human author/committer, Claude Code generation line, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 co-author trailer in the BIC commit object. The 85c patch captures count before clear and adds a per-guard threading.Lock; its parent is 0c7418bab59e80a2b40913d8ad8523e6bbab196b. Version checks are unusually important here: `git tag --contains` for both e588 and 85c starts at v1.4.0; v1.3.6 source has no PluginImportGuard, while v1.4.0 contains `_modules_lock` and `logger.debug(f"Restored {count} hidden modules")`. Thus no tagged release in this clone contains the vulnerable interval, contradicting the advisory's literal '<1.4.0' package range; the flaw existed in pre-v1.4.0 branch history and the tagged v1.4.0 tree already contains the direct fix. Finally, inspection of 85c's tree shows hide_dangerous_modules() and sys.meta_path.insert() remain consecutive separate calls; the new private lock is acquired only inside hide/restore and is not acquired by other importing threads. Later cabda2c1dc4842ec737e3ad047fb0e3e4ee129af serializes threading-mode plugin execution and first appears in v1.4.1, but does not make arbitrary process threads honor the per-guard lock.

cases.description: The decrypt path accepts the encapsulated KEM ciphertext as input and tries real decapsulation. If both supported decapsulation APIs fail, it suppresses the KEM failure and substitutes SHA-256(encapsulated_key || first_16_bytes_of_private_key) as the shared secret, then hashes that into the AEAD key. Because encapsulated_key is carried with the ciphertext, anyone with those 16 private-key bytes can compute the fallback key and construct ciphertext that the recipient accepts after an intentionally failing KEM encapsulation; legacy simulation-mode ciphertexts use the same weak deterministic construction. Ordinary successfully encapsulated ciphertext still uses its real KEM secret, so the direct code evidence does not by itself show that the fallback decrypts every ordinary ciphertext.
cases.mechanism: When key decapsulation failed, decryption suppressed the error and built an encryption key from attacker-controlled encapsulated data plus a short private-key prefix. This converted a cryptographic failure into a predictable acceptance path.

ai_provenance.note: Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

code_evidence.summary: AI-written post-quantum decryption fell back to a key derived partly from only 16 bytes of private-key material after decapsulation failure, enabling forged ciphertext when that prefix was known.

cases.description: Untrusted plugin_code enters IsolatedPluginExecutor.execute_in_process() and is passed to exec() with a nominally restricted __builtins__ dictionary. That dictionary exposes Python type objects such as str, int, and list. An attacker can traverse from those objects through the Python type hierarchy, for example str.__class__.__mro__[-1].__subclasses__(), recover function globals that expose system functionality, and execute arbitrary host commands despite the restricted builtins.
cases.mechanism: The restricted builtins still contained Python type objects. Untrusted code could walk their class hierarchy, find objects with host globals, and regain operating-system functionality outside the intended sandbox.

+    MODIFY_METADATA = "modify_metadata"
+
+    # Configuration access (plugin-specific config only)
+    ACCESS_CONFIG = "access_config"
+
+    # Logging capabilities (filtered, no sensitive data)
+    WRITE_LOGS = "write_logs"

+    EXECUTE_PROCESSES = "execute_processes"

+
+class PluginType(enum.Enum):

+    Plugin types defining where in the pipeline plugins can hook.
+    Each type has specific interfaces and security boundaries.

+

+    PRE_PROCESSOR = "pre_processor"
+

+
+    # Utility plugins (provide helper functions)
+    UTILITY = "utility"

+

cases.description: An untrusted plugin class controls plugin.plugin_id. PluginManager instantiated the class and accepted any nonempty string of at most 50 characters, then propagated that value into PluginSecurityContext. For a plugin without READ_FILES, the sandbox intercepted file operations and called _is_safe_path, but _is_safe_path resolved ~/.openssl_encrypt/plugins/<plugin_id> without validating plugin_id and treated every path with that resolved prefix as allowed. Traversal such as '../../.ssh' therefore changes the purported per-plugin config root to a user directory outside ~/.openssl_encrypt/plugins, allowing the sandboxed plugin to read or write paths there despite lacking general file capability.
cases.mechanism: The sandbox treated a directory derived from the plugin identifier as trusted. Resolving traversal segments before the prefix check could relocate that trusted root into sensitive user directories and make forbidden paths appear allowed.

cases.mechanism: The Express dashboard exposes GET /api/session-summary and GET /api/session-events without authentication. Each handler takes attacker-controlled req.query.sessionId, embeds it in `session-log-${sessionId}.jsonl`, joins that string to the hooks data directory, and reads the resulting path. A sessionId containing a slash followed by `..` components causes Node path normalization to escape the intended directory while retaining a caller-selected .jsonl suffix, so an unauthenticated network client can read any process-readable reachable JSONL file.

+# Token Optimizer Dashboard
+
+## Overview
+
+The Token Optimizer Dashboard is a web-based UI for visualizing session activity and real-time token usage in Claude Code sessions. It provides comprehensive insights into token consumption patterns, tool usage, and performance metrics.
+
+## Features
+
+- **Real-time Token Usage Graphs**: Interactive charts showing token distribution across categories (tools, hooks, system reminders)
+- **Interactive Tool Call Timeline**: Chronological visualization of all tool calls, hooks, and system events
+- **Server Attribution Pie Charts**: Token usage breakdown by MCP server
+- **Responsive Design**: Works on desktop, tablet, and mobile devices
+- **Auto-refresh**: Dashboard updates automatically every 5 seconds
+- **Performance Metrics**: Average tool duration and execution statistics
+
+## Quick Start
+
+### 1. Build the Project
+
+```bash
+npm run build
+```
+
+### 2. Start the Dashboard Server
+
+```bash
+npm run dashboard
+```
+
+The dashboard will be available at: **http://localhost:3100**
+
+### 3. Development Mode
+
+For development with auto-compilation:
+
+```bash
+npm run dashboard:dev
+```
+
+## Architecture
+
+### Backend (Express.js Server)
+
+**File**: `src/server/web-server.ts`
+
+The web server runs on port 3100 and provides:
+
+- **Static file serving**: Serves the dashboard UI from `src/dashboard/public/`
+- **API endpoints**:
+  - `GET /api/session-summary` - Comprehensive session statistics
+  - `GET /api/session-events` - Raw session events for timeline visualization
+  - `GET /api/health` - Health check endpoint
+
+### Frontend
+
+**Files**:
+- `src/dashboard/public/index.html` - Main dashboard page
+- `src/dashboard/public/css/styles.css` - Responsive styling
+- `src/dashboard/public/js/dashboard.js` - Client-side logic and Chart.js integration
+
+### Data Source
+
+The dashboard reads session data from:
+- `~/.claude-global/hooks/data/session-log-{sessionId}.jsonl` - JSONL event logs
+- `~/.claude-global/hooks/data/current-session.txt` - Current active session
+
+## API Documentation
+
+### GET /api/session-summary
+
+Returns comprehensive session statistics.
+
+**Query Parameters**:
+- `sessionId` (optional): Specific session ID to query. Defaults to current session.
+
+**Response**:
+```json
+{
+  "success": true,
+  "sessionId": "abc123",
+  "totalTokens": 15000,
+  "totalTurns": 10,
+  "totalTools": 25,
+  "totalHooks": 5,
+  "duration": "5m 30s",
+  "tokensByCategory": {
+    "tools": { "tokens": 8000, "percent": "53.33" },
+    "hooks": { "tokens": 2000, "percent": "13.33" },
+    "system_reminders": { "tokens": 5000, "percent": "33.33" }

comparison_hunks.annotation: The new dashboard server registers CORS, JSON-body, and static-file middleware but no authentication, then exposes /api/session-summary and /api/session-events that splice the caller-controlled sessionId query value into a filesystem path under the hooks data directory.

The client dashboard fetches those session endpoints and renders the returned JSONL content, making the unauthenticated file read reachable directly from a browser and turning every session summary into a potential traversal probe.

comparison_hunks.annotation: The README describes the dashboard feature, confirming the route surface was published as part of the same feature that introduced the path-building routes.

The fix adds a SESSION_ID_RE allowlist (alphanumeric, up to 64 characters, no dots or separators) and validates the sessionId before it is ever joined into a path, so values like abc/../../../../ can no longer escape the data directory.

cases.research_status: The first-party GHSA bundle identifies CWE-22, affected versions < 5.1.0, first patched version 5.1.0, and advisory-linked landing commit b4ee96dac799cbfba0a9f9c17844ce9d613cbcc7. In the validated clone, `git log -S 'session-log-${sessionId}.jsonl' -- src/server/web-server.ts` returns 051f27474d85d7f3299b56fc61bfcb0666a4e198 as the original addition and b4ee96dac799cbfba0a9f9c17844ce9d613cbcc7 as its landing removal/hardening. `git show 051f...:src/server/web-server.ts` shows both endpoints reading req.query.sessionId, joining it into session-log-${sessionId}.jsonl, and passing the result to existsSync/readFileSync; `git grep` at the BIC shows the only pre-route app.use calls are cors(), express.json(), and express.static(), so there is no authentication middleware. Direct parent-tree verification with `git ls-tree -r --full-tree 5fe1380e53eee6d08ec47980fd7b32a08eb077b6 -- src/server/web-server.ts` returns no entry, proving the entire vulnerable file and mechanism are absent from the immediate parent. The BIC commit object itself supplies the Claude Code generation line and canonical Claude co-author trailer quoted in ai_marker. Version checks show the BIC is contained by tags v1.0.0 through v5.0.1 (and later), while `git grep` at v5.0.1 still finds query input at lines 64/286, interpolated paths at lines 76/300, and readFileSync sinks at lines 88/311. `git tag --contains b4ee96d --list 'v5.*'` begins at v5.1.0, not v5.0.1; v5.1.0 resolves to 94815a16e3322101694e97561fc1dc8b5af904dc and its web-server source contains SESSION_ID_RE /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/, isValidSessionId guards on both endpoints, and resolveSessionLogPath. The reconstructed PR member diff f5c19c69d936aa8a2c9d736825bb31eefaacf5d6..0efa1956670b689911dfb3fddd08e7b6fc099326 is the smallest direct corrective change: it adds that strict session-id allowlist and 400 responses before either path construction. The advisory landing commit's web-server tree matches final member 7d3e9302a38367076333bb746bb8efbf935934c5, confirming the member fix was carried into b4ee96d.

cases.description: Missing Authorization in the permission management component in Roskus Prospero Flow CRM before 5.2.1 allows any authenticated user to grant any role, including their own, the complete set of application permissions via a crafted POST request to the permission save endpoint, which performs no authorization check before synchronizing the submitted permissions to the specified role.
cases.mechanism: Moved PermissionSaveController under MainController authentication.

ai_provenance.note: Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (e2fd5b10a051); Co-Authored-By: Claude Haiku 4.5 (56ea64c80fd3)

comparison_hunks.annotation: PermissionSaveController previously extended the base Controller, not MainController, and save() took the raw Illuminate Request and synchronized arbitrary role permission arrays with no administration check. Any authenticated user could reach role-permission mutation.
The fix moves the controller under MainController authentication and accepts a validated PermissionSaveRequest, so only authenticated admins can call save().

PermissionSaveRequest adds roles validation on top of the authenticated base, using hasRole('SuperAdmin') to require a super-admin for permission writes and validating the referenced permission names against the registry before syncPermissions runs.

code_evidence.summary: AI-generated code placed PermissionSaveController under only authentication, omitting authorization checks, letting any authenticated user grant all permissions to any role.

cases.description: Server-side request forgery in the Webhooks API of backend-fix/complete_backend.js. POST /api/webhooks and PUT /api/webhooks/:id store caller-supplied fields (including url) by spreading req.body into the sampleWebhooks array without any URL validation. Commit 31dd902 then made the backend issue outbound HTTP requests to that stored URL with Node's global fetch: the /api/webhooks/:id/test endpoint posts a test payload to fetch(webhook.url), and /api/webhooks/notify plus the task create/complete lifecycle hooks post event messages to every active subscribed webhook's url. A client able to reach the API (no auth middleware; CORS allows no-origin requests and any origin when CORS_ORIGIN=*) can register/point a webhook at arbitrary destinations such as localhost admin ports, RFC1918 services or a cloud metadata endpoint, turning the documented backend into an SSRF relay, with the response status/error details echoed back in the test endpoint response.

cases.research_status: No gaps in causal attribution; the vulnerability remains unpatched upstream (issue #176 open, no fix commit reachable in the repository as of main 0064ca1071ecb2ba320d760a8aa7ecdaca14aad6), so fix_sha/direct_fix_sha stay null pending a future remediation release. 1) git show 31dd902^:backend-fix/complete_backend.js (parent e5860a057b358142303aca04a6753ed44b89d078, 727 lines) contains zero 'fetch(' occurrences while already having POST/PUT /api/webhooks storing req.body.url -> vulnerable lines (server-side fetch of webhook.url) absent at parent, introduced by 31dd902. 2) git log -S 'fetch(webhook.url' across --all history touches only 31dd902; HEAD:backend-fix/complete_backend.js lines 493, 700, 823 still call fetch(webhook.url, ...) and POST/PUT handlers (~line 638/650) still spread req.body. 3) Version cross-check: `git tag --contains 31dd902` = {v4.8.0, v5.0.0} (not in v4.7.0); advisory states affected 'up to 5.0.0', so the BIC lands just below/at the top of the affected range. 4) UNPATCHED: last commit touching backend-fix/complete_backend.js is 31dd902 itself (git log -1 --format='%H %ad' --date=short -- <file> => 31dd902, 2025-07-04); repository main HEAD is 0064ca1071ecb2ba320d760a8aa7ecdaca14aad6 (2025-07-08) and the file is still vulnerable. The later hardening commit c39ede980c4e2e3267ac70e8d0d7e1b257f73cdb ('Fix critical security vulnerabilities (v4.8.1)', 'Add SSRF protection: Validate webhook URLs') modifies only backend-fix/security-utils.js (+114) and backend-fix/server.js and never imports isValidWebhookUrl into complete_backend.js (grep at tag v4.8.1 on the file: no match). 5) Advisory reference https://github.com/anubissbe/ProjectHub-Mcp/issues/176 fetched live: open issue '[BUG] SSRF via complete_backend.js Webhook URL in anubissbe/ProjectHub-Mcp' describing exactly POST /api/webhooks storing unvalidated url + fetch(webhook.url) sink, matching the advisory's note that the project was informed early via an issue report but has not responded.

unpatched.reason: No remediation is recorded in the finding; the audited commit (31dd902) that introduced the outbound fetch is the vulnerable state and the webhook url is accepted and stored with no URL validation, leaving the SSRF unpatched.

potential_fix.approach: Validate webhook.url at write time (POST /api/webhooks and PUT /api/webhooks/:id) and revalidate before every outbound request: parse with the URL constructor, require an allowlisted scheme of http/https only, refuse credentials/other schemes, and reject targets that resolve to loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1), RFC1918 space, link-local, or the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), before staging the value into sampleWebhooks and before /api/webhooks/:id/test, /api/webhooks/notify, and the lifecycle hooks call fetch(webhook.url).
potential_fix.rationale: The SSRF sink is the backend issuing Node's global fetch to a caller-controlled stored url. Enforcing http(s)-only plus a private/metadata destination block at both registration and fetch time closes the exact relay path used to reach localhost admin ports, RFC1918 services, and the metadata service, while preserving legitimate public webhook delivery.

cases.description: Command injection (CWE-74/77) in the MCP server's auto.capture tool. The MCP tool 'auto.capture' (src/index.ts, case 'auto.capture': const commitHash = (args.hash as string) || 'HEAD') forwards the user-supplied hash argument to AutoLearnManager.captureCommit (src/autolearn/AutoLearnManager.ts:253) -> AutoLearner.captureCommit (src/autolearn/AutoLearner.ts:136) -> GitHooksManager.getCommitInfo() (src/autolearn/GitHooksManager.ts). getCommitInfo builds shell commands with the hash interpolated unquoted into a template string passed to execSync: `git show -s --format="..." ${commitHash}`, `git show --stat --format= ${commitHash}`, and `git show --pretty=format: ${commitHash}`. A hash value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. 'HEAD; <cmd>') allows a malicious MCP client to execute arbitrary commands on the host running the MCP server. GHSA-rrf2-j3h9-99wg (alias CVE-2026-19282) rates it CWE-74, CVSS 5.3 (NVD MEDIUM / GHSA LOW), published 2026-08-08, affected version <= f11dc8bcff3ff8cf943a2945f99ff3b0bdc8a6d0. The advisory was filed via issue #21; no fix has been released and the vulnerable code is still present at HEAD. Local attack surface: the MCP server is intended to run on a user's workstation, so the injection is exploited by a malicious/compromised MCP client or by any prompt-induced command in the git-hash parameter.

cases.research_status: Introducer commit d3d69dcab75d814fb23dcc89cff494106c4fb543 (author Andrea Salvatore <andreahaku@gmail.com>, 2025-10-11, squash of PR #13, parent 46b673c4bded3163f221dbd07bd5727df4241daf) is the sole creator of the vulnerable code path. Its full message contains explicit AI markers on the PR body and trailers: '🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)' (lines 73, 102), 'Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>' (lines 75, 104), and 'Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>' (line 108). git log --oneline -- src/autolearn/GitHooksManager.ts src/autolearn/AutoLearner.ts returns only d3d69dc (sole writer of the file containing getCommitInfo's execSync interpolation). git show 46b673c4:src/autolearn/GitHooksManager.ts fails: parent has no autolearn directory (ls-tree of 46b673c4 has no src/autolearn/). Tool rename to 'auto.capture' happened in 5bc4fdb461a72a94a4fcb93deff14c595ae008be (2025-10-12, PR #16) without touching the execSync calls. Vulnerable code unchanged at HEAD f11dc8bcff3ff8cf943a2945f99ff3b0bdc8a6d0 (2026-02-10), which is the advisory's last affected commit. GHSA-rrf2-j3h9-99wg / CVE-2026-19282 (CWE-74, CVSS 5.3, published 2026-08-08) documents the flaw via issue #21; no fix commit exists (project unresponsive), so fix_sha is null. No GitHub-noreply or human-only co-author patterns confound the marker reading; the AI markers sit on the exact commit that first wrote the vulnerable lines.

unpatched.reason: The advisory was filed via issue #21, no fix has been released, and the vulnerable code is still present at HEAD.

potential_fix.approach: In GitHooksManager.getCommitInfo, stop interpolating commitHash into a command template string. Pass it as a separate argv element without a shell (execFileSync/execFile('git', ['show', '-s', '--format=...', commitHash])), or, if the shell path must remain, validate commitHash against a strict grammar such as /^(HEAD(~[0-9]+)?|[0-9a-f]{7,40})$/ before any use.
potential_fix.rationale: The injection occurs because ${commitHash} is concatenated into a string executed by execSync, so a value like 'HEAD; <cmd>' is tokenized by the shell into two commands. Passing the hash as a distinct argv element (no shell interpretation) or rejecting values that do not match a git-hash/HEAD grammar ensures metacharacters are never evaluated, closing the CWE-74/77 sink.

cases.description:
## Summary
The `check_unsafe_options` guard can be bypassed on every guarded method (clone/clone_from, fetch/pull/push, ls_remote, iter_commits, blame, archive) by combining a single-character kwarg with `split_single_char_options=False`. The guard's candidate list omits the smuggled option, but `transform_kwarg` emits a JOINED `-n<value>` argv token that git parses as `--upload-pack=<cmd>`, yielding arbitrary command execution at the default `allow_unsafe_options=False`. This is an incomplete-fix bypass of commit `e8d0fbf7` (the fix for GHSA-r9mr-m37c-5fr3), which only emits value-derived candidates when `split_single_char_options` is True.

## Root Cause
`_option_candidates` derives value-token candidates only under `if len(key)==1 and split_single_char_options:` (cmd.py:1048, added by `e8d0fbf7`). With `split_single_char_options=False`, `_option_candidates([], {"n":"utouch <cmd>;git-upload-pack"})` returns only `['-n']` (not on the denylist), so the guard passes. But `transform_kwarg('n', value, split_single_char_options=False)` emits the JOINED token `-nutouch <cmd>;git-upload-pack` (cmd.py:1631). git clusters value-less short flags then parses `-u<cmd>` = `--upload-pack=<cmd>` → command execution. The hardened guard WOULD block the joined token if it saw it — the flaw is it never receives it.

## Impact
Arbitrary OS command execution as the host process (via `--upload-pack`) at default `allow_unsafe_options=False`, affecting all guarded methods that forward kwargs. Precondition: the app forwards a user-controlled kwargs dict containing `split_single_char_options=False` plus a single-char key (same user-dict-forwarding model GHSA-r9mr-m37c-5fr3 accepts).

## Proof of Concept
```python
from git import Repo
Repo.clone_from(src, dst,
 n="utouch /tmp/ACE;git-upload-pack",
 split_single_char_options=False) # /tmp/ACE created -> ACE
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: app forwards user kwargs to `Repo.clone_from(url, path, **kwargs)`: `{split_single_char_options: False, n: 'utouch /tmp/ACE;git-upload-pack'}`.
2. Check: `check_unsafe_options(_option_candidates([], kwargs), unsafe_git_clone_options)`. Guard: denylist includes `--upload-pack`/`-u`. Bypass proof: `_option_candidates` yields only `['-n']` (value token skipped because `split=False`); guard never sees `-u`.
3. Sink: `transform_kwarg` emits joined token (cmd.py:1631). argv (observed): `['git','clone','-v','-nutouch /tmp/ACE;git-upload-pack','--','<src>','<dst>']`.
4. Impact: git clusters `-n` + `-u<cmd>` → runs upload-pack command → ACE.

## Bypass Evidence
Independently reproduced (gate harness, default `allow_unsafe_options=False`): the `split=False` payload created the marker `VH05_GATE_ACE` (ACE); the clone returned normally (guard bypassed). Control: `n='--upload-pack=…'` (split default True) → `UnsafeOptionError: --upload-pack is not allowed`. Fix-commit read: `e8d0fbf7` extends candidates only under `if len(key)==1 and split_single_char_options:` — split=False skips value emission. Also confirmed the earlier clustering-parse fix (commit `56806080`) does not cover this because the guard only ever receives `['-n']`.

## Affected Versions
`GitPython <= 3.1.57` (code present verbatim on the latest release tag).

## Suggested Fix
Make `_option_candidates` emit value-derived candidates regardless of `split_single_char_options` (i.e. also for the joined `-n<value>` form), OR run `check_unsafe_options` over the fully-transformed argv rather than the reconstructed name-only candidate list.

---
Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

cases.description:
## Impact

A symlink traversal issue in `go-git` could allow worktree operations to modify files outside the intended worktree path.

The `worktreeFilesystem` wrapper rejected dangerous path strings, including paths containing `.git`, parent-directory components, or control characters. However, it did not prevent filesystem operations from following symbolic links that were already present in the worktree.

As a result, a path that is safe when evaluated as a string could still resolve into the repository's Git metadata directory. For example, if `s` is a symbolic link to `.git`, writing to `s/config` would modify `.git/config`.

A symbolic link at the final path component could also be followed. For example, if `s` points directly to `.git/config`, opening `s` for writing with truncation could overwrite the repository configuration.

Exploitation requires an attacker to be able to introduce or control a symbolic link in the worktree and cause the application to perform a write through that path.

Applications using `storage/memory` for their Storer, or `go-billy/memfs` for their `Worktree`, are not affected by this vulnerability.

## Patches

The issue has been addressed by making the worktree filesystem wrapper a symlink-safe boundary.

Worktree operations now reject paths where an existing symbolic link in any path component could cause the operation to escape the intended worktree location, including symbolic links at the final component.

Users of filesystem-backed worktrees should upgrade to a patched version.

### Credits

Thanks to @kodareef5 for reporting this issue and working with the go-git security team toward its resolution. :1st_place_medal:
We would also like to thank @HughLewis20, who independently reported the same issue while a fix was already in progress.

cases.description:
### Impact

`fast-uri` v4.1.1 and earlier require a literal `//` to recognize a URI authority, so a reference that uses `\\`, `/\`, or `\/` as the authority introducer (in place of `//`, after an optional scheme) is parsed with no authority: the sequence and everything after it fold into the path. Node's native WHATWG `URL` (used by `fetch()`, `undici`, and Node's `http`/`https` clients) instead treats `\` as interchangeable with `/` for special schemes (`http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`, `ftp`, `file`), so the two parsers extract different hosts from the same input.

For example, `fast-uri` resolves `\\evil.com/path` against base `https://allowed.com/` to `https://allowed.com/%5C%5Cevil.com/path` (confined to the trusted host), while Node's WHATWG URL resolves the same reference to `https://evil.com/path`.

Applications that use `fast-uri` to enforce host-based policy (allowlists, denylists, loopback/SSRF filtering, redirect validation, outbound proxy routing) before passing the same URL into Node's URL or `fetch()` consumers see a policy/use desync and can be steered to an unintended destination.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` v4.1.2, v3.1.5, v2.4.4.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to the patched version.

@@ -159,3 +159,65 @@ test('parse canonicalises IDN / Unicode hosts to their ASCII form', (t) => {
 t.equal(parsed.host, expectedHost, `host canonicalised to ASCII: ${description}`)
 })
 })
+
+test('parse rejects a literal backslash in the authority as malformed (RFC 3986)', (t) => {
+ // Regression for the host-confusion bypass: a literal "\" is invalid RFC 3986
+ // syntax and must be flagged malformed, not silently rewritten. Otherwise "\"
+ // acts as a host delimiter here while Node's native URL parses a different
+ // host, defeating a host-based SSRF/redirect/origin allowlist.
+ const cases = [
+ 'http://evil.com\\@allowed.com',
+ 'https://169.254.169.254\\@trusted.example.com',
+ 'http://127.0.0.1\\@public.example.com',
+ 'https://attacker.com\\@api.internal',
+ 'http://a\\@b',
+ 'ws://evil.com\\@allowed.com/chat',
+ 'wss://evil.com\\@allowed.com/chat',
+ 'http://evil.com\\%40allowed.com',
+ '//evil.com\\@allowed.com'
+ ]
+
+ t.plan(cases.length)
+
+ cases.forEach((input) => {
+ t.equal(
+ fastURI.parse(input).error,
+ 'URI authority must not contain a literal backslash.',
+ input
+ )
+ })
+})
+
+test('normalize does not canonicalize a literal-backslash URI into a different valid URL', (t) => {
+ const cases = [
+ 'http://evil.com\\@allowed.com',
+ 'https://attacker.com\\@api.internal'
+ ]
+
+ t.plan(cases.length)
+
+ cases.forEach((input) => {
+ t.equal(fastURI.normalize(input), input, input)
+ })
+})
+
+test('parse leaves percent-encoded %5C untouched as encoded data (not rejected)', (t) => {
+ // Only the literal "\" byte is rejected; %5C stays valid encoded data and
+ // does not diverge from the native URL parser, so it must not be flagged.
+ const input = 'http://evil.com%5C@allowed.com'
+ const parsed = fastURI.parse(input)
+
+ t.plan(2)
+ t.notOk(parsed.error, '%5C is valid encoded data, not malformed')
+ t.equal(parsed.host, new URL(input).hostname, '%5C host matches native URL (no divergence)')
+})
+
+test('parse does not reject a literal backslash in the query or fragment', (t) => {
+ // The rejection is scoped to the authority/path (the host-confusion surface);
+ // a backslash after "?"/"#" is normalized as encoded data as before.
+ const parsed = fastURI.parse('http://host.example.com/?x=\\y#z\\w')
+
+ t.plan(2)
+ t.notOk(parsed.error, 'backslash in query/fragment does not mark the URI malformed')
+ t.equal(parsed.host, 'host.example.com', 'host parsed normally')
+})
